notes.meaning: The prophet is commanded to deliver a message to the mountains of Israel. Because the people were taken away to Babylon, Ezekiel speaks directly to the land itself. Earlier in the book God spoke warnings against these hills, but now he sends them a word of comfort. God has not forgotten his promised country even while it lies empty.

Surrounding nations celebrated when Jerusalem fell and claimed the ancient hill country for themselves. Edom especially mocked God's people and boasted that the land was now their own prize. These enemies assumed that God had abandoned his covenant promises. God heard their proud boasting and prepares to answer it.

Foreign neighbors rushed in like hungry animals to swallow up the deserted territory. They gossiped about Israel and turned God's land into a cruel joke. The ruined nation became a byword, meaning that people used its name only to mock it. God noticed every slanderous whisper and insult spoken against his people.

The Lord speaks directly to every feature of the landscape, including hills, ravines, and deserted towns. These areas had been plundered and mocked by the nations living nearby. God calls the land to listen because he still cares for every broken valley and ruined street. His love extends to the very soil where his people once lived.

The Lord declares in fierce zeal that he will confront Edom and the other greedy nations. These neighbors had taken God's land for themselves with spiteful joy and deep contempt. God calls the territory his own land, reminding everyone that it belongs to him rather than to those who stole it. His burning passion is set against those who mistreated his inheritance.

Ezekiel must assure the hills and valleys that God's fiery anger is stirred up on their behalf. The land had suffered the shame of foreign mockery for a very long time. God's deep affection for his land moves him to intervene. He will not allow that public humiliation to continue forever.

The Lord raises his hand to make a solemn oath. He promises that the neighboring nations who laughed at Israel will soon bear their own disgrace. God turns the tables so that the bullies suffer the exact shame they poured out on others. His judgment is completely fair and sure.

God commands the mountains of Israel to sprout new branches and grow fruit for his people. The time of exile in Babylon is almost over, and the people will soon journey home. God prepares the land ahead of time like a home waiting for its family. The soil is told to be ready to feed the returning exiles.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe this promise looks beyond the return from Babylon to a future time when Israel will enjoy physical blessings in Christ's earthly millennial kingdom.

notes.meaning: The Lord declares that he is on the side of the land and is turning his favor back to it. Instead of lying wild and neglected, the hillsides will be plowed, planted, and cared for once again. God replaces his past anger with tender care for the soil. His blessing brings fruitful life where there had only been neglect.

God promises to multiply the population across the hills, gathering the entire family of Israel back together. Ruined cities will be rebuilt from the rubble and filled with living communities. God restores the whole nation rather than leaving pieces behind. His blessing restores daily life and security to places that were abandoned.

Both people and livestock will greatly multiply across the land. God promises to make Israel even more prosperous than it was in its earliest days. This great renewal will show the people beyond any doubt that the Lord is faithful to his word. God's kindness exceeds the good things they had enjoyed before.

God will bring his people back to walk upon the hills as their permanent family inheritance. In past years, war and starvation made the land seem like a trap that robbed parents of their children. God promises that the land will no longer take away their sons and daughters. Instead, it will be a secure home where families grow and thrive.

Foreign neighbors spread a bad report that the land devoured its own inhabitants. This taunt recalled the fearful report of the spies during the time of Moses, who said the land swallowed people up. Disasters like famine and warfare had given the region an unhealthy reputation. The surrounding peoples thought the soil itself brought disaster.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers view the dramatic agricultural growth and greening of the land of Israel since 1948 as the beginning of the fulfillment of these verses.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises that the land will never again devour its people or take away their children. The deadly trials of starvation, disease, and war will no longer consume the population. God removes the root cause of the trouble so the curse is broken. His people can rest securely under his protection.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers view the dramatic agricultural growth and greening of the land of Israel since 1948 as the beginning of the fulfillment of these verses.

notes.meaning: God will silence the cruel taunts of the foreign nations once and for all. Israel will no longer have to carry the heavy burden of public shame or stumble under divine judgment. When God defends his people, he wipes away the insults that once crushed their spirits. His peace guards them against foreign contempt.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers view the dramatic agricultural growth and greening of the land of Israel since 1948 as the beginning of the fulfillment of these verses.

notes.meaning: The Lord speaks to Ezekiel once more to begin a new part of the message. Before describing the spiritual gifts he will give, God explains why Israel had to go into exile in the first place. He wants the people to understand the truth about their past so they can appreciate his grace. True healing begins with an honest look at sin.

When Israel lived in the land, the people defiled it by their wicked behavior. In the worship laws, uncleanness meant being unfit to enter God's holy presence, like someone needing ceremonial washing. Israel's continual rebellion made the holy land unacceptable to God. Sin always ruins the blessings and good places God provides.

God poured out his wrath on his people because they murdered the innocent and worshiped worthless idols. Bloodshed and false gods deeply polluted the land God had set apart for himself. God's holiness could not overlook such deliberate wickedness. His judgment was a necessary response to their ongoing rebellion.

The Lord drove the people out and scattered them across the nations as exiles. This dispersion was a fair judgment that matched the evil they had done. God held them accountable according to the covenant laws they had agreed to follow. His justice was completely right and balanced.

Wherever the exiles went, their presence dishonored God's holy name among the nations. The heathen peoples assumed the Lord was too weak to protect his people or keep them in his land. Israel's defeat gave outsiders a false impression of who God really is. The people's fall damaged the Lord's reputation among their neighbors.

The Lord felt deep concern for the honor of his own holy name. His name stood for his perfect character, truthfulness, and power, which Israel had brought into disrepute. God resolved to rescue them, not to reward them, but to clear his name of every false accusation. He acts to make his true holiness visible to the world.

Ezekiel is told to give the house of Israel a blunt and humbling message. God will not act because they deserve it or have earned his favor. He will act entirely for the sake of his holy name, which they dishonored among the nations. Salvation is rooted in God's mercy rather than human goodness.

The Lord will show the nations that his great name is truly holy. When God cleanses and restores his people in plain view, foreign nations will finally recognize that he is the one true God. His holiness will shine through the way he deals with his people. God vindicates his character by saving unworthy sinners.

God promises to gather his scattered people out of every foreign country and lead them back to their homeland. He will not leave them lost among the nations where they were exiled. This gathering shows that God is faithful to his ancient promises to their ancestors. His power reaches into every land to bring his children together.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this prophecy points to a future literal return of Jewish people to the land of Israel in the end times.
Many evangelicals believe this was partly fulfilled after the Babylonian exile and points ultimately to God gathering all believers into Christ's church.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises to sprinkle clean water on his people to make them pure. Under Old Testament laws, sprinkling water washed away ritual filth so a person could worship God. Here it represents God forgiving sins, cleansing the conscience, and freeing them from all their idols. God provides the inner washing that people cannot give themselves.

differ.view: Lutherans see this clean water as pointing forward to baptism, through which God washes away sin and works new birth.
Baptists view this sprinkling as a symbol of spiritual cleansing through the blood of Christ and the Spirit, rather than the sacrament of baptism.

notes.meaning: God promises to give his people a new heart and a new spirit, taking away their stubborn heart of stone and replacing it with a heart of flesh. A stony heart is cold, hard, and uncaring toward God, while a heart of flesh is tender, living, and responsive. This gift is regeneration, which means being given brand-new spiritual life from God. Only God has the power to change a human heart from the inside out.

differ.view: Reformed Christians teach that God sovereignly gives the new heart first, so that spiritual rebirth comes before a person can exercise faith.
Methodists teach that God offers grace to all, and he gives the new heart when a person willingly responds in faith.

notes.meaning: The Lord promises to place his own Holy Spirit inside his people. Instead of forcing obedience from the outside through written rules, the Spirit will move their wills so they gladly obey God's commands. God's Spirit provides both the desire and the strength to live a holy life. Real obedience is the fruit of God working within us.

differ.view: Pentecostals emphasize that the Spirit within leads to the empowering baptism in the Holy Spirit, enabling dynamic Christian witness and obedience.

notes.meaning: The renewed people will live securely in the land God promised to their forefathers. There they will experience the heart of God's covenant: they will be his people, and he will be their God. Spiritual renewal and fellowship with the Lord go together. Belonging to God brings true safety and peace.

God promises to rescue his people from all their uncleanness and provide plentiful food. He will summon the grain like a master calling a servant, ensuring that famine never attacks the land again. God cares for both the spiritual purity and the physical needs of his people. His salvation brings wholeness to every part of life.

The orchards and fields will produce abundant harvests so hunger will never return. Surrounding nations will no longer have reason to mock Israel for facing starvation. God replaces old disgrace with visible generosity and care. His provision removes the shame of poverty.

When the people taste God's overwhelming grace, they will remember their old sins with deep grief and self-loathing. True repentance does not come from terror, but from realizing how good God has been to people who did not deserve it. Remembering God's mercy melts hard hearts and turns them away from evil. Grateful sorrow keeps believers humble.

The Lord repeats with great emphasis that he is not doing any of this because they deserve it. He tells Israel to feel ashamed and disgraced for their wicked choices. God wants his people to abandon all self-righteous pride. Grace is entirely unearned, so all glory belongs to God alone.

On the very day God cleanses his people from their sins, he will also rebuild their ruined towns and fill them with residents. Inner forgiveness and outward renewal belong together in God's restoration plan. God heals the lives of his people and restores the communities where they dwell. His mercy brings order out of devastation.

Fields that lay deserted and overgrown in the sight of every traveler will be plowed and farmed once again. Passersby had once stared in shock at the complete ruin of the countryside. Now those same roads will run past rich and cultivated crops. God turns public ruin into a public witness of his restoration.

Travelers will be astonished and say that the ruined land has become like the Garden of Eden. Towns that were once burned and smashed will stand strong with new walls and bustling crowds. God's creative power turns an empty wilderness into a place of beauty and safety. His work brings paradise where there had been only death.

The neighboring nations that survive will realize that the Lord alone rebuilt the ruins and replanted the wasteland. What God says with his mouth, he accomplishes with his power. His fulfilled promises show everyone that he is the living, active God. God's faithfulness to his word displays his glory to the whole world.

The Lord announces that he will allow the house of Israel to pray and ask him for these promised blessings. Even though God has already promised to multiply them, he invites his people to seek him in earnest prayer. God honors prayer as the way his children express faith and dependence. What God promises in grace, his people should ask for in faith.

The rebuilt cities will be as crowded with people as Jerusalem was with sacrificial sheep during the great religious feasts. These huge flocks of people are not just numerous; they are dedicated as living offerings to the Lord. In the end, everyone will know that the Lord is the true and faithful God. God fills his kingdom with people who belong entirely to him.
